new_statements.quote: 8. (stress placement) In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase. [examples: /tiŋaŋ/ → [tiˈŋaŋ] 'hornbill'; /daraʔ/ → [daˈraː] 'long, of time'; /balatup/ → [balaˈtup] 'inflate'; /kalasuʔ/ → [kalaˈsuː] 'steam'; /mataʔ+ndo/ → [ˈmatandoː] 'sun']

new_statements.rule_in_words: In isolation (citation form) a word is stressed on its final vowel/syllable; inside a phrase stress shifts to the penultimate syllable. Affixes are monosyllabic and normally unstressed; full words bear stress (p. 20). Cubit 1964 (p. 415) says the same for Baram Kayan: non-phonemic, usually on the last syllable of 2- and 3-syllable words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Blust; Cubit 1964 (Baram) says words of more than three syllables are 'usually [stressed] on the last two syllables' and 2-syllable words may occasionally carry stress on both syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Blust: stress is penultimate within the phrase (positional, not lexical); the rapid-speech locative marker /haʔ/ is never stressed. Cubit: fluctuation between first and second syllable in disyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms vs phrase-internal forms explicitly distinguished (final in citation, penult in phrase). Cubit treats stress as non-phonemic with emphasis (length/fortis) phonemic.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Uma Juman Kayan of the Balui branch of the Rejang River, Sarawak = Rejang Kayan (Glottolog reja1241, ISO ree), NOT Kayan Mahakam (kaya1324, xay). The parallel Cubit 1964 statement (p. 415, stress non-phonemic, usually final) describes the Uma Pu dialect of Long Atip, Baram = Baram Kayan (bara1370, ISO kys). Both are sister languages in the Kayan subgroup; Guerreiro 1996 (fn. 3, p. 207) notes Kayan Mahakam of Long Kuling was creolised with Pin speech and is not mutually intelligible with Busang, so transfer of the rule to xay is a hypothesis, not a description. No first-hand phonological description of xay itself was found.

readall_conflicts: No source opened describes Kayan Mahakam (xay) itself, so no conflict on the catalog item. Among the neighbouring varieties: Barth 1910 (Busang Kayan, busa1255) gives a light word-final accent with phrase-final placement in sentences ('op de laatste lettergreep van het laatste woord'); Blust 1977 (Uma Juman, Rejang Kayan) gives word-final stress in citation but penultimate stress within the phrase; Cubit 1964 (Baram Kayan) gives non-phonemic, usually final stress. The word-level readings agree (final); the phrase-level readings of Barth and Blust differ (phrase-final last syllable vs. penultimate).

sources.note: P. 76, P-rule 8 (stress placement): 'In citation forms the last vowel of a word receives stress. Stress is penultimate within the phrase.' Also p. 20 (general): stress falls on the final syllable of citation forms but the penult in context in most languages described. Variety = Uma Juman, Balui branch of the Rejang, Sarawak (Rejang Kayan, reja1241), not Kayan Mahakam.
